title: Interleaving
content_html:
Mixed practice

Interleaving

Mix topics in one session — don’t block them.

What the Research Says

Most students revise by blocking — an hour on the Olympians, an hour on Mycenae, an hour on the Odyssey episodes. It feels productive and the topic seems clear by the end. Interleaving is the opposite: you jump between topics inside a single session. It feels worse at the time, and you’ll make more mistakes. But when the real exam arrives, you will be dramatically better at knowing which concept to apply — and that is usually the hardest part of any Classical Civilisation question.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Rohrer & Taylor (2007)Students who interleaved topics scored 43% higher on delayed tests than blocked-practice students.Same time spent — huge difference in exam performance.
Birnbaum et al. (2013)Interleaved learners felt LESS confident during practice but performed BETTER in the test.If revision feels too easy, interleave.
Bjork & Bjork (2011)Desirable difficulties — including interleaving — create durable long-term learning at the cost of short-term performance.Short-term struggle is the price of long-term gain.
Taylor & Rohrer (2010)Benefit was largest when topics looked superficially similar — students learnt to DISTINGUISH them.Most useful where students confuse similar concepts.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Pick 3–5 related topics — topics that share a paper, a theme, or a question type. Similar enough that students confuse them.
  2. 2
    Make a mixed question set — 10–15 questions drawn randomly from all the topics. Don’t tell yourself which topic each question belongs to.
  3. 3
    Attempt each question cold — first step is identifying what’s being asked. That identification is the skill you’re training.
  4. 4
    Mark after every question — note which topic each one was. Pay attention to mis-identifications — those are the highest-value gaps.
  5. 5
    Rebuild a new mixed set tomorrow — same topics, different questions. Different order. Over time, misclassifications drop.
  6. 6
    Expect to feel worse than blocked practice — that’s the right feeling. Your exam self will thank you.
Example 1

Create a 15-question mixed set spanning Myth & Religion topics: the twelve Olympians and their attributes, the labours of Heracles, Greek temple architecture and the three orders (Doric, Ionic, Corinthian), religious festivals, foundation myths, and the geography of the underworld. Because all of these relate to Greek religion and myth, exam questions can sound deceptively similar. Working through them in random order forces you to identify whether a question asks about a specific deity, an architectural feature, a festival practice, or a mythological narrative — a distinction that separates short-answer identification marks from developed analytical responses.

Example 2

In the final weeks before the exam, interleave Myth & Religion source questions (for example, “What does this image of Heracles tell us about how the Greeks viewed heroism?”) with Homeric World source questions (for example, “What does the Cyclops episode reveal about the importance of xenia in Homeric society?”). Switching between literary analysis and material-culture analysis in one sitting closely mirrors the actual exam experience, where students must identify which type of source they are analysing — literary, visual, or archaeological — before they can deploy the right analytical approach.

Common Pitfalls

  • Random, not related. Interleaving Classical Civilisation with Geography is just subject-switching. Interleave WITHIN Classical Civilisation — related concepts that students confuse, such as Greek and Roman names for the same gods, or architectural orders.
  • Giving up when it feels hard. The discomfort is the signal that it’s working. Don’t revert to blocked practice because interleaving feels slow.
  • Labelling the topic at the top of each question. Defeats the point — the identification IS the training.
  • Using it too early in learning. You need baseline familiarity with each topic first. Interleaving is for consolidation, not first exposure.

When to Use This

Once you’ve covered a handful of related topics — usually partway through a term — start weaving them into mixed practice sessions. Very useful in the final 8–10 weeks before exams when you’re moving from learning to applying. Full past papers are the ultimate interleaving exercise, because they force you to identify question types cold and decide whether to draw on literary, visual, or material evidence.

Quick Reference
~30–45 minutes per session

  2. Build a mixed set
  3. Attempt cold
  4. Mark & note topic
  5. Fix misclassifications
  6. Expect discomfort
